description_en: A temple in Koṭilā and dedicated to Koṭeśvara Mahādeva.The site of Koṭilā is located on a small hill laying, south-west of the larger hill where stands Nārāyaṇa, Dailekh' district headquarter (also known as Dailekh Bazār). It is situated at the confluence of the Koṭilā Kholā (now mostly dry) coming from the north-east and the Chhāmghāṭ Kholā coming from the north-west.The site used to have a natural flame. Adhunifire ritually replaces the extinguished natural flame. The Koṭeśvara Mahādeva Temple is located on top of the Koṭilā hill.Koṭilā is part of an area know as Pañcakośī. The sites of the Pañcakośī are visited by pilgrims from all over western Nepal. The sites are notorious for their flame temples (natural gas flames), said to mark places where Satī's body parts fell while Śiva carried her charred body (Lecomte-Tilouine 2009). Koṭilā is the place where Satī's ears fell. This is one of the starting places of the Pañcakośī pilgrimage.Access to the temple is made by walk up a flight of concrete stairs passing by different shrines, including a small Bhairam temple and a temple of Bhagavatī Mālikā temple adjoining a temple of Sūrya. The top of the narrow hill is crowned by a flat area comprising a pillared pavilion (maṇḍapa) containing thedhunifire, built in front of the Śiva Temple. The temple is built of concrete imitating a brick pattern. It has only one room, thesanctum, accessed through a door in the south-east wall. A stoneśivaliṅgais placed on a pedestal at the centre of thesanctum. A simple colonnade runs around the temple. Saṃnyāsi women take care of thedhunifire and Śiva Temple.Behind the temple, to the west, is a terrace area paved with cement. At the foot of a tree are a few carved stone blocks (002, 003 and 004). Another carved block, containing a bas-relief image of Gaṇeśa, is placed to the right side of the temple's door (001). One of the carved stone blocks was probably a memorial pillar. It bear an inscribed dated reading:sa 1822. If this date in the Vikrama Samvat (VS), it corresponds to the year 1765 CE. The other artefacts may also be dated from the 18th-19th century.The site is discussed inLecomte-Tilouine 2009and inPokharel 2011, p. 110-111.
